newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish peacebroker Hume to fight British election.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish peacebroker Hume to fight British election.

text.p: Northern Ireland peace broker John Hume announced on Saturday -- his 60th birthday -- that he would stand again in forthcoming British elections to continue his efforts to bring peace to the troubled province.

Hume, head of the Irish nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) said in a statement he was "committed to continuing his work at Westminister (the British parliament) and at other fora to bring lasting peace to this island."

The statement ended speculation among pro-British politicians in Northern Ireland and pro-Irish nationalists about whether Hume, who helped broker a 1994 Irish Republican Army (IRA) ceasefire, would contest the seat he has held since 1979.

It also scotched suggestions that the seat, based around Northern Ireland's second city, Londonderry, might fall to Sinn Fein, the militant voice of Irish nationalism and political wing of the IRA guerrillas.

Hume's Catholic-backed SDLP represents moderate Irish nationalists who want the peaceful reunification of now British-ruled Northern Ireland with the overwhelmingly Catholic Irish Republic from which it was partitioned 70 years ago.

Hume has been in poor health in recent years and has complained of a heavy workload due to his peace-broking role and work at the British parliament, as well as being the only Irish nationalist with a seat in the European Parliament.
The SDLP has four seats at Westminster compared with 13 held by its ideological rivals, the Unionists, who represent the 60 percent Protestant majority who want Northern Ireland to stay British.
British Prime Minister John Major must hold elections by May 22 this year. Opinion polls say Major's Conservatives look sure to lose to the opposition Labour party.

Hume, whose quest for peace has earned him recognition in Washington as well as a nomination for the Nobel peace prize, helped draft a plan for settling the 28-year-old Northern Ireland conflict with Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams in 1993.

It led the British and Irish governments to draw up their own blueprint, the Downing Street Declaration of December 1993, which said Britain would not oppose Irish reunification so long as a majority of people in Northern Ireland approved it.
This helped lay the foundations for an August 1994 ceasefire by the IRA in its war against British rule.

But the guerrillas abandoned their truce in February last year, complaining that Britain was creating hurdles to Sinn Fein's participation in multiparty peace talks by insisting that all guerrillas disarm to prove commitment to democracy.
Hume said this month that Irish nationalists deserved a bigger voice in the British parliament but ruled out any electoral deal with Sinn Fein until the IRA called a new truce.
